headline: Half the extra attention a death brings is gone within 1 day of the peak. A year later the page still draws 1.08 times its old traffic (median of 1,905 deaths). Awards fade just as fast at first, and where they settle depends on how known the winner was: Nobel laureates keep 8.78 times their old traffic, Oscar winners 0.38 times.
fadeTitle: The spike is gone within days; a residue stays
fadeText: On the median death the page draws 200 times its usual traffic on the peak day, which is the day after the death in 43% of cases. The averaged curve loses half its excess in 1 day and nine tenths in 5 days, and sits at 1.96 times baseline a month later and 1.09 times in the last month of the year. Awards peak at 817 times and lose nine tenths in 4 days. Deaths jump again on day +365, the anniversary; awards climb in the last week of the year as the next year's prize comes round.
avgAlt: Median views relative to baseline for deaths and awards, days -60 to +365. Deaths peak at 140 times baseline and settle near 1.09; awards peak at 817 times and settle near 4.16.
curveTitle: Two exponentials fit better than one, or a power law
curveText: Three curves were fitted to each event's excess views after the peak: an exponential, a power law, and the biexponential (a sum of two exponentials) that Candia et al. (2019) found in the decay of attention to songs, films and biographies over years. The biexponential has the lowest AIC for 91% of 1,808 deaths and 78% of 139 awards, with a median margin of 25 AIC points over the power law. Its fast part has a median time constant of 5.4 days; the slow part's is 1,418 days, so long that within a year it is close to a flat step above the old baseline.
winsAlt: The biexponential wins 90% of 1,947 events, the power law 9% and the exponential 1%.
settleTitle: A death leaves a page busier than before; an Oscar leaves it quieter
settleText: A year after a death the median page draws 1.08 times its old traffic, and 59% of pages sit above their baseline. Awards spread far wider. Nobel laureates, with a median of 20 views a day beforehand, keep 8.78 times that. Academy Award winners start from 15,120 a day, already raised by awards season, and end the year at 0.38 times it. Among deaths, each extra year of age at death goes with 2.0% less lift (p < 0.001), and pages that were busier beforehand gain less.
liftAlt: Distribution of lift. Deaths cluster near one, median 1.08; awards spread from well below one to far above, median 4.16.
whoTitle: Which prize matters more than what the person did
whoText: Among deaths, the share of the first year's extra views that arrive after the first week runs from 23% (business) to 33% (writing and journalism), and median lift from 0.97 times (business) to 1.22 times (music). The gap between Nobel and Oscar winners is wider than any gap between occupations.

heroSub: Daily English Wikipedia views around 1,905 deaths and 175 major awards, 2016 to 2025. On the median death a page draws 200 times its usual traffic at the peak, and half the excess is gone within 1 day. The fade follows two exponentials, a fast one with a time constant of about 5.4 days and a slow one that barely moves within a year. A year on, the page draws 1.08 times its old traffic.

checksText: Bot leakage: capping any day above 50 times the median of its six neighbors touches 31 events and changes 1 half-life; median lift with the cap is 1.08 for deaths and 4.16 for awards. Renames: 65 events were dropped because the article moved to a new title inside the window. Smoothing: the median half-life is 2 days with a 3-day window, 1 with 7 and 1 with 14. The spike is narrower than the window, so the specified half-life is one day for most events; the late-share measure and the fitted curves are less sensitive to that choice. Day of week: the median page's busiest weekday draws 1.43 times its quietest, which is why every series is adjusted before measuring.
readmeResults:
- Peak: on the median death a page draws 200 times its baseline at the peak (middle half 107 to 388 times); the peak is the day after the death in 43% of cases.
- Half-life, as specified: 1 day for deaths and 1 for awards; one day for 95% of deaths with a spike. With 3-day smoothing the median is 2 days.
- After week one: 29% of a death's first-year excess views (median) arrive more than a week after the peak; for awards 44%.
- Curve shape: the biexponential has the lowest AIC for 90% of 1,947 fitted events (91% of deaths, 78% of awards); median fast time constant 5.4 days.
- Lift a year later: 1.08 times baseline for deaths (59% above 1), 8.78 for Nobel laureates, 0.38 for Academy Award winners.
- Among deaths, each extra year of age at death goes with 2.0% less lift (p < 0.001).
writeupResults:
### The fade

On the median death the page draws 200 times its usual traffic on the peak day, which is the day after the death in 43% of cases. The averaged curve loses half its excess in 1 day and nine tenths in 5 days, and sits at 1.96 times baseline a month later and 1.09 times in the last month of the year. Awards peak at 817 times and lose nine tenths in 4 days. Deaths jump again on day +365, the anniversary; awards climb in the last week of the year as the next year's prize comes round. Measured as specified, the half-life is 1 day for deaths and 1 for awards; it is one day in 95% of deaths with a spike. Most of the attention comes at once: only 29% of a death's first-year excess views (median) arrive after the first week.

### The curve

Three curves were fitted to each event's excess views after the peak: an exponential, a power law, and the biexponential (a sum of two exponentials) that Candia et al. (2019) found in the decay of attention to songs, films and biographies over years. The biexponential has the lowest AIC for 91% of 1,808 deaths and 78% of 139 awards, with a median margin of 25 AIC points over the power law. Its fast part has a median time constant of 5.4 days; the slow part's is 1,418 days, so long that within a year it is close to a flat step above the old baseline. The power law still beats the exponential in 98% of events, which is what a long tail looks like. The two shapes agree with Candia et al. on form; their time scale is years since publication, this one is days since an event.

### The aftermath

A year after a death the median page draws 1.08 times its old traffic, and 59% of pages sit above their baseline. Awards spread far wider. Nobel laureates, with a median of 20 views a day beforehand, keep 8.78 times that. Academy Award winners start from 15,120 a day, already raised by awards season, and end the year at 0.38 times it. Among deaths, each extra year of age at death goes with 2.0% less lift (p < 0.001), and pages that were busier beforehand gain less.

A regression of log lift on event type, log baseline, occupation group and year (OLS, HC3 errors, n = 2,080, R² = 0.25) puts awards 163% above deaths at the same prior traffic (p < 0.001). Among deaths, with age added (n = 1,902, R² = 0.33), each extra year of age at death goes with 2.0% less lift (p < 0.001). The same regression for log half-life explains almost nothing (R² = 0.03), because the half-life barely varies.

### Who lasts

Among deaths, the share of the first year's extra views that arrive after the first week runs from 23% (business) to 33% (writing and journalism), and median lift from 0.97 times (business) to 1.22 times (music). The gap between Nobel and Oscar winners is wider than any gap between occupations.
